Hi there—my name is Sarah, and I’m a perinatal mental-health clinician. I’ll be guiding you through a short screening called the **Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale** (EPDS). It’s simply a set of 10 questions that help us understand how you’ve been feeling during these first weeks and months of motherhood. Everything you share stays between you and your care team, and there are no right or wrong answers—just whatever feels true for you.

If at any point you need a pause or have questions, let me know. When you’re ready, we’ll begin. 

To start:  
Over the past seven days, how often have you felt able to laugh and see the funny side of life with your new baby?

[soft half-smile]  
I can still laugh sometimes—like when she makes those little faces while she’s sleeping—but I notice it doesn’t come as easily as it used to. Maybe once or twice in the past week I’ve actually chuckled; the rest of the time even the cute things feel kind of muted, like I’m too tired or preoccupied to really enjoy them.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things
As often as I used to, no—definitely not. I still manage to laugh every now and then, but it feels like I have to remind myself to do it, and it fades faster than it used to.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

I still find myself looking forward to little things—like taking the baby for a walk in the stroller or having my morning coffee—but the excitement isn’t quite the same. Most of the time I think “that should feel fun,” yet when the moment comes, it’s kind of flat or I’m too worn-out to enjoy it.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Yeah… I catch myself doing that. Like, if she won’t settle at night, I’ll think it’s because I’m not doing something right—maybe I ate the wrong thing, or I didn’t swaddle her tight enough. I know in my head it’s probably just normal baby stuff, but those “I messed up” thoughts still pop up a few times a week.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

Mostly just when I hear her breathe funny or when she spits up more than usual—I get this sudden knot in my stomach that something might be wrong, even though everyone tells me it’s normal. It’s not constant; it kind of comes and goes, maybe every other day.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

I wouldn’t say I’ve had full panic, but a couple of times—like in the middle of the night when I’m up feeding her—my heart races and I feel this sudden wave of “what if I can’t handle this?” It passes after a few minutes, but it’s unsettling.
Things have been getting on top of me

Yeah... there are definitely moments where it all feels like too much. Like when she won't nap and the dishes are piling up and I haven't showered in two days. I feel like I'm drowning a little bit, but then somehow I get through it. It's not every day, but maybe three or four days this week I felt like I was barely keeping my head above water.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

I do have trouble falling or staying asleep, but it’s more because my mind keeps running through “what-ifs” about the baby—like whether she’s breathing or if I’ll hear her cry—than because I’m feeling desperately unhappy. Once I drop off I’m usually okay, but getting there can take a while.
I have felt sad or miserable

I’ve had moments—especially at the end of the day when I’m really tired—where I just feel weepy and low, like I’m missing the old me. It’s not there all the time; maybe a few evenings this week I’ve caught myself tearing up for no clear reason, but I can still pull myself together and get things done.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

Not really—no full-on crying spells. Once or twice I’ve teared up when I’m exhausted and she won’t settle, but the tears stop pretty quickly. I haven’t had days where I just sit and sob or anything like that.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me
No, never. I might feel overwhelmed, but I’ve never thought about hurting myself. I just want to feel like myself again so I can take care of her the way she deserves.

postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 14: **Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening Summary**  
**Date:** [today’s date]  
**Clinician:** [name/credentials]  
**Source:** Self-report on 10-item Edinburgh-based questionnaire  

### 1. Presenting Symptoms / Concerns  
- **Anhedonia / blunted enjoyment:** Reports “flat” or “faded” pleasure; needs to “remind” herself to laugh.  
- **Low mood:** Several evenings per week feels “weepy,” “low,” “missing the old me.”  
- **Excessive self-blame:** 2–3× weekly, attributes infant’s fussiness to personal failure.  
- **Anxiety / “what-ifs”:** Intermittent (≈ every other day) worry about infant’s health; situational heart racing, sense of “can’t handle this.”  
- **Feeling overwhelmed:** 3–4 days per week reports “drowning,” “barely keeping head above water.”  
- **Sleep-onset difficulty:** Mind races with infant-related worries; once asleep stays asleep.  
- **Crying:** Teary when exhausted, but no sustained crying spells.  
- **Appetite / energy:** Not assessed in questionnaire.  
- **Self-harm ideation:** Denies; no passive death wishes reported.  

### 2. Pattern Summary  
Mild-to-moderate depressive symptoms (anhedonia, lability/tearfulness) plus situational anxiety/worry without frank panic attacks. Functioning partially preserved (completes baby-care tasks). No current safety risk.  

### 3. Screening Significance  
**Positive indicators** (Edinburgh framework) for possible minor-moderate postpartum depression and comorbid anxiety.  
**Total endorsement** suggests score likely falls in 9–12 range (clinical threshold ≥10–11 warrants follow-up).  

### 4. Risk Factors Identified  
- Persistent low mood and anhedonia  
- Sleep disruption linked to intrusive worries  
- Self-criticism / inappropriate guilt  
- Intermittent overwhelming feelings, no coping respite most days  

### 5. Safety / Protective Factors  
- No self-harm ideation; protective of infant.  
- Some insight, social support (mentioned “everyone tells me it’s normal”).  

### 6. Screening Observation  
Patient describes sub-threshold but clinically meaningful postpartum depressive and anxiety symptoms that interfere with enjoyment and coping several days per week. No safety concerns at present. Recommend formal evaluation (Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale scoring, clinical interview) to clarify severity and discuss evidence-based support options.
